title: A One-Dimensional Energy Balance Model Parameterization for the Formation of CO2 Ice on the Surfaces of Eccentric Extrasolar Planets
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how the formation of carbon dioxide (CO2) ice on cold, eccentric exoplanets affects planetary climate and habitability. The authors note that existing climate models have typically represented ice-albedo feedback using water ice alone, even though CO2 can condense at sufficiently low temperatures and may substantially change planetary reflectivity. The central question is whether adding a CO2 ice-albedo parameterization changes the predicted climate stability of Earth-like planets across different stellar environments and orbital eccentricities.

To answer this, the authors modify a one-dimensional energy balance climate model to include a CO2 ice-albedo parameterization alongside existing treatments of land, ocean, and water ice. They run simulations for Earth-like planets orbiting F-, G-, K-, and M-dwarf stars under warm-start and cold-start conditions, varying orbital eccentricity, stellar flux, and CO2 ice grain size. The model is also validated against approximate Earth and Mars climates and used to estimate transitions into snowball states, deglaciation thresholds, and runaway greenhouse conditions.

The study finds that including CO2 ice generally increases planetary albedo and strengthens climate hysteresis, especially for planets orbiting brighter stars. F-dwarf planets require substantially more instellation to thaw than in water-ice-only simulations, while M-dwarf planets are less affected in the thawing threshold. Eccentricity reduces the tendency to remain fully glaciated because periastron heating promotes deglaciation, and larger CO2 ice grains lower albedo and make thawing easier. Overall, the paper concludes that CO2 ice should be included in climate models of cold and eccentric planets because it materially changes predicted habitability and climate stability.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed scientific modeling paper in astrobiology, not an education study. It does not evaluate any educational technology, intervention, learners, or learning outcomes, so none of the K-12 evidence credibility criteria apply.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact because it studies planetary climate modeling and CO2 ice-albedo effects on exoplanet habitability, not student learning, instruction, or educational systems.
